3.3 — Fire Rate: Cooldowns & Time

Last lesson your turret did not fire shots, it fired a stream — every frame, for as long as you stood in range. Today it learns to wait, using a number that gets spent.

Search terms for this lesson“in unity how to stop a turret firing every frame, how to make a cooldown with time.time, how to fire on an interval”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The turret should shoot at me — but not sixty times a second. "Shoot at me, sometimes" is the whole feature, and there is nothing in it yet that a computer can act on.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Know the player is still inside the radiusThe answer 3.1 already keeps in inRange — set true by OnTriggerEnter2D() and false by OnTriggerExit2D(). A turret that asks "is the player close?" every frame is re-asking a question the collider already answered.Read: the inRange field and the two trigger callbacks in your own 3.1 script.
  2. write this partRead: the Time.deltaTime row in the quick reference, and the default value rule from 1.3.
  3. Spend the clock once per frame, and only while it matterstimer -= Time.deltaTime; inside if (inRange). Each frame hands over its own duration, so after a second of frames the timer is a second smaller — at any frame rate.Read: the Time.deltaTime row in the quick reference, and the if shape from 1.4.
  4. Fire at zero, then refill the whole intervalif (timer < 0) opens the gate and timer = timeBetweenShots closes it again. One line spends, the other resets — the pair is the whole cooldown.Read: the Cooldown row of the pattern table in the quick reference.

Three of the four parts are code you have already written. The one with no precedent in this course is the memory: a field that is slowly spent rather than counted.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, in one search? "Fire less often" cannot be looked up. "Subtract the frame time from a number each frame" can.

Your turn

The table in the code half prices four ways to time this action. Which did you choose, and what does your choice cost you — in your own words, not the table's?

Today's memory is spent down to zero and refilled. If the turret had to charge for a second before each shot instead, what would the field mean while it was charging — and which of the four approaches would you reach for?

In the Editor ~10 min
  1. Game view → press Play and stand inside one turret's radius for five seconds, then Console → count the lines that appear. Write the number down: it is the rate your frames are running at, not a decision anybody made.
  2. Project window → Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs, then Game view → press Play and watch the Scene view: the fireballs leave the muzzle in one clump per frame, faster than you can read.
  3. Once the walkthrough is done — Project window → TurretController.cs, set timeBetweenShots to 2, save, and press Play, then time ten shots against a stopwatch. It is a float in the script, so tuning is an edit and a new play — the same rule as speed in 1.5, not an Inspector box.
  4. Hierarchy → the two Turret instances, and stand between them: with the interval in the script, both turrets keep time identically. If you want one to be slower, you need a second value — see the callout in the code half.
Build Lab: Pick a Timing Model ~35 min
Approach What you store The gate What it costs you
(a) A Time.time timestamp One float: the moment the last shot happened. Time.time >= lastShot + interval The clock runs whether or not the turret cares, so a player who leaves and comes back ten seconds later is shot immediately — the cooldown paid itself while nobody was there.
(b) A countdown timer — this project One float: seconds remaining until the next shot is allowed. timer < 0, then timer = interval Something has to tick it down, every frame, and you have to decide what the tick means outside the radius. In exchange it reads as "seconds until I can shoot", which is what you want to see while tuning pacing.
(c) InvokeRepeating Nothing at all — the engine holds the schedule. InvokeRepeating(nameof(Shoot), 0f, interval) Almost no code, and that is the trap: your method is called on cadence whether or not the player is in range, so the range check has to move inside it. Cancelling is by method name, so a rename breaks the cancel silently.
(d) A coroutine loop A running coroutine handle. while (true) { yield return new WaitForSeconds(t); } A StartCoroutine() call, a stored handle to stop it, and a second mental model of when your code runs. It is the only row that expresses "charge, then burst, then rest" cleanly.
Why this project takes (b). The turret's trigger already tells it when the player is in range, and row (b) is the only one that can be ticked inside that answer. The cost is the callout below, and it is a real one: the two rows do not behave the same when the player walks away mid-cooldown.
The frozen clock. The tick sits inside if (inRange), so the countdown stops while the player is outside the ring. Leave at 0.8 seconds remaining and come back ten minutes later, and the turret still owes 0.8 seconds. Row (a) would not do that — its clock never stops. Neither behaviour is wrong; one is a turret that saves your progress and the other is a turret that reloads on its own. Know which yours is, because a player will notice.
In the CodeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I stop shooting too fast?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs. Your 3.1 and 3.2 turret does not change: the trigger still sets inRange, and Shoot() still spawns a fireball at the muzzle. Today adds a knob, a countdown, and the two lines that spend it.

This build leaves 2 lines for you to write. Everything around them is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Declare the knob and the countdown

Both lines go in the class body, outside every method — the placement rule from 1.3.

// TurretController.cs — class body, above Start(), with your other fields.
    float timeBetweenShots = 1.5f;

    float timer;
  1. 2The knob: how many seconds must pass between shots. A plain float, so it is tuned by editing this line and playing again — the same choice speed makes in 1.5.It has to be a float. An int cannot hold 1.5; it would round to 1, and a turret tuned to fire twice a second would quietly fire once a second, from a type nobody sees on screen.
  2. 4The memory: one float holding the seconds still owed before this turret may fire again. It shrinks every frame the player is in range, and jumps back to the knob after each shot.Where this line lives is the memory. Move it inside the method that reads it and it is rebuilt from nothing every frame, holding the same empty value each time. That is the scope rule from 1.3: the same line in the wrong place is not a memory, it is a habit.

Step 2Start the countdown full

Once, before any frame has run.

// TurretController.cs — inside Start(), with your 3.1 target setup.
        timer = timeBetweenShots;
  1. 2The countdown begins at a full interval, exactly as if a shot had just left.The first shot is a design decision, not a default. Starting at 0 would make the turret fire the instant the player crossed the ring — a free shot for a turret the player never got to see. Starting full means every visit costs the same first second.

Step 3Spend the countdown while the player is in range

The inRange answer is your 3.1 field. Today it stops being the thing that fires and becomes the thing that lets time run.

// TurretController.cs — inside Update(), on the inRange check from 3.1.
        if (inRange)
        {
            ______________________________

            if (timer < 0)
            {
                Shoot();

                ______________________________
            }
        }
  1. 2The gate is the 3.1 field, unchanged. Everything inside these braces runs only while the player is inside the ring.
  2. Your turn4Spend one frame's worth of time. Write the line that takes this frame's duration off the countdown.The frame's duration is the Time.deltaTime row in the quick reference — you multiplied by it in 1.4 to make speed per-second. Here the same number is subtracted instead.This is the whole countdown. Time.deltaTime is the wall-clock seconds since the previous frame — around 0.017 at 60 fps, twice that at 30. Subtract it every frame and after one real second you have subtracted one second, whatever the machine did in between. That is why it is -= and not -= 1: subtracting 1 would spend the timer in one frame, and the turret would fire every frame again.
  3. 6The gate: the countdown has run out. < 0 rather than == 0 because the tick almost never lands exactly on zero — it steps past it. "At or past empty" is what < 0 says.
  4. 8Your firing method from 3.2 — the one that spawns a fireball at the muzzle and hands it target. Unchanged, whatever you named it.
  5. Your turn10Refill the countdown so the next shot costs the same interval again. This runs only when a shot has actually left the barrel.The field holds seconds remaining, and the knob holds how many seconds a full interval is. What assignment puts it back to full?The most common bug in this lesson. Leave it out and the timer keeps going negative: the gate stays open on the next frame and every frame after, and the turret is back to firing at your frame rate — the bug you started with, rebuilt inside the fix.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it: your names, your interval, your spawn and your 3.1 trigger are yours, and the shape is what has to match. If you built the Time.time stamp instead, you have implemented row (a) — a real answer, and not the one this project chose.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class TurretController : MonoBehaviour
{
    float timeBetweenShots = 1.5f;      // the knob: seconds between shots
    float timer;                        // the memory: seconds still owed

    bool inRange = false;               // set by the Detection Radius trigger
    Transform target;                   // who walked in

    [SerializeField] GameObject fireballPrefab;
    [SerializeField] Transform spawnPoint;

    void Start()
    {
        // ...your 3.1 detection and targeting stays as it is...

        timer = timeBetweenShots;       // a full interval before the first shot
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (inRange)
        {
            timer -= Time.deltaTime;    // spend one frame's worth of time

            if (timer < 0)              // at or past empty
            {
                Shoot();

                timer = timeBetweenShots;   // refill: the gate closes again
            }
        }
    }

    void Shoot()
    {
        // ...the projectile spawn you wrote in 3.2, unchanged...
    }
}
Build Lab: Your Row ~10 min
Architectural specification — for whichever row you chose.
  • The knob. Which float sets the gap between shots, and what default will you ship for it? A plain field is tuned in the script; [SerializeField] would put it in the Inspector so one turret could differ from another. Say which you used and what you gave up.
  • The memory. What does your row keep between frames — a moment, a duration, a handle, or nothing the engine is not already holding — and why can it not live inside the method that reads it?
  • The gate and the reset. Which two conditions must both be true before the turret may fire, and which of them comes from a trigger callback rather than a comparison? What changes at the instant a shot actually leaves?

Choosing a Timing Model

  1. Trace your own 3.2 build: standing inside the radius for one second, how many projectile clones did your firing method create — and why did that number depend on the machine rather than on you?
  2. Why can't you call a "wait one second" function inside Update()? Describe what the player would see on screen during that wait, and explain why a game engine refuses to let you block the frame.
  3. Row (a) stores a moment; row (b) stores a duration. Which one can you print in the Console and have a player immediately understand, and which one is easier to compare against a designer's tuning value? Then say which this project took, and what it gave up to get there.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break "the turret should not fire every frame" into its parts, and name the earlier lesson you lifted each one from
  • Explain why your turret was firing once per frame, naming the line responsible
  • Compare the four timing approaches, state what each one costs, and give a reason for your choice that is about this behaviour
  • Explain why the refill line is mandatory, what bug returns without it, and why the tick is timer -= Time.deltaTime rather than timer -= 1
  • Say what the countdown does while the player is outside the radius, and whether that is what you want
